title: A Drone Just Hit Oman's Largest Oil Terminal. India's Hormuz Bypass Is No Longer Safe.
excerpt: The explosion at Mina al Fahal extends the Middle East conflict beyond the Strait of Hormuz and into the open-ocean infrastructure India was counting on to keep crude flowing.
body:
An explosion near the single-buoy mooring berths at Oman's Mina al Fahal crude terminal has forced a halt to oil loading operations at one of the Gulf state's primary export facilities, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters on Friday. The blast, attributed to an alleged drone attack, struck between the terminal's SBM 1 and SBM 2 berths. Several supertankers were seen anchored offshore, unable to load.

The timing could not be worse for India. Mina al Fahal sits on the Gulf of Oman, outside the Persian Gulf, in waters that were supposed to be the safe alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The strait has been largely closed since the US-Iran war began three months ago, severing a waterway that once carried a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies. India had been actively rerouting its energy imports through Oman, signing a landmark trade pact with Muscat just days ago that was designed to bypass the Hormuz chokepoint entirely.

That calculation now looks dangerously optimistic.

## The Zone of Risk Is Widening

Until this week, the direct disruption to export infrastructure had been concentrated around the Strait of Hormuz itself. Drone attacks had previously struck Oman's Duqm port and Salalah terminal in the early days of the conflict, but Mina al Fahal is different. It handles roughly one million barrels per day of Omani crude, priced at around $121 per barrel, well above the global benchmark Brent, which trades near $97.

The incident extends the conflict's reach into open-ocean terminal infrastructure beyond the strait, a development that will unsettle energy traders and military planners across Asia. For India, the world's third-largest crude importer, the implications are immediate. New Delhi has spent weeks scrambling to secure alternative supply lines from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria. The India-Oman trade pact was meant to anchor a Gulf supply corridor that avoided the most dangerous waters. A drone attack on the very terminal that corridor depends on undermines the entire strategy.

## Oman's Diplomatic Role Under Threat

The geopolitical dimension is as significant as the supply disruption. Oman has occupied a uniquely valuable position throughout the conflict, maintaining open lines of communication with both Washington and Tehran and serving as one of the few credible neutral venues for back-channel diplomacy. The sultanate played a similar role during earlier rounds of nuclear negotiations with Iran.

Any erosion of Oman's status as neutral ground, whether through direct targeting or the spillover effects of a widening war, would remove one of the few remaining diplomatic pressure valves the region has left. Iranian state media reported on Wednesday that Tehran targeted a US military vessel in the Gulf of Oman, a claim US Central Command denied. The escalation pattern, however, is unmistakable.

## What This Means for Indian Households

The rupee has already slid to become Asia's worst-performing currency in 2026, and crude oil prices have surged more than 45 percent since February. Every dollar increase in the price of a barrel of oil adds roughly $2.1 billion to India's annual import bill. If loading operations at Mina al Fahal remain suspended for any length of time, the disruption will ripple through petrol pumps, LPG cylinder prices, and household budgets across the country.

The Reserve Bank of India is announcing its monetary policy decision today, with most economists expecting the central bank to hold its repo rate at 5.25 percent. But the Oman attack adds a new variable to an already impossible equation. Governor Sanjay Malhotra must now weigh the inflationary shock of a widening energy disruption against the drag on growth from an economy already under strain.

For India's energy planners, the lesson of Mina al Fahal is stark: in a war that has already closed the world's most important oil chokepoint, there may be no such thing as a safe bypass.
